https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/news/uk-wo.text: The Trump administration is reportedly allowing the extradition of Andrew Tate and his brother Tristan to Britain. The US president apparently has no plans to step in to intervene after the pair were arrested in Miami on Saturday by US police at the request of British detectives, reports The Telegraph . The pair now face being brought back to the UK where they face a litany of alleged sexual offences including rape and human trafficking. When the Tate's were first arrested in Florida last year following a period of house arrest in Romania, Andrew suggested in leaked texts that the Trump administration had helped him and his brother to flee the country. Trump said he knew "nothing about it" when he was asked about this at the time, reports The Mirror. Their latest arrest was met with calls from some leading Republican figures and administration individuals for Trump to step in. The brother's lawyer, Joe McBride has claimed they are victims of a "politically motivated witch hunt". The Telegraph has now said a US official told the paper that the White House will not get involved in the case. The official reportedly said: "The White House has no involvement and no feelings on the issue." The pair have "unequivocally" denied wrongdoing, with Andrew Tate describing himself and his brother as "very innocent men". A total of 38 new charges were authorised against Andrew Tate, 39, and Tristan Tate, 38, by the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS). Andrew Tate was charged with seven further counts of rape, three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation, three counts of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and 19 additional charges for offences relating to indecent images of a child and extreme pornography. Tristan Tate was charged with one count of sexual assault, two counts of rape and three counts of arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation. Charges were previously authorised by the CPS following a file of evidence submitted by officers from Bedfordshire Police into allegations dating back to 2012. Bedfordshire, Cambridgeshire and Hertfordshire Major Crime Unit have been continuing to investigate a number of other alleged offences reported to both Bedfordshire Police and Hertfordshire Constabulary. The total number of charges against the brothers now totals 59. Of these, 42 charges have been authorised against Andrew Tate, and 17 against Tristan Tate. The CPS confirmed it had requested the extradition of Andrew and Tristan Tate from the US. Malcolm McHaffie, head of the CPS's Special Crime Division, previously said: "We have decided to prosecute Andrew and Tristan Tate for further offences including rape, arranging or facilitating trafficking for sexual exploitation and offences relating to indecent images of a child. "These charging decisions followed receipt of a further file of evidence from Bedfordshire Police and bring the total number of alleged victims in this case to seven." The offending is alleged to have taken place between July 2010 and August 2017, according to the CPS.

Ezt majd a friss inflációs jelentés ismeretében dönti el a Monetáris Tanács. A magyar jegybanki alapkamat sokáig 6,25 százalékon állt, az áprilisi választások utáni befektetői bizalom azonban teret nyitott a lazításnak. A Varga Mihály vezette MNB június végén élt ezzel először, minimális mértékben, 6,25-ről 6 százalékra vitte le a kamatot . A lépést az is indokolta, hogy a választás utáni optimizmusban annyira megerősödött a forint, hogy az már az exportáló cégek versenyképességét rontotta, a megkérdezett vállalkozások 17 százaléka mondta , hogy három hónapig sem bírja 355 forintos euróárfolyam mellett. Studying the coldest place in Utah could help combat inversions Mountain West News Bureau | By Brock Marchant Published September 28, 2026 at 8:31 PM MDT Facebook LinkedIn Email Listen • 2:11 Brock Marchant / UPR | The Salt Lake Tribune András Dobos (left) and Utah State University graduate research assistant Tim Wright install a temperature sensor at Peter Sinks in Logan Canyon on July 29, 2026. Peter Sinks in Logan Canyon gets remarkably cold. Here's how scientists say that could teach us about inversions. In 1985, the second-coldest temperature ever recorded in the Lower 48 was reached in Utah. The frigid air, collected at the basin of Peter Sinks in Logan Canyon, had dropped to 69.3 degrees below zero before Zane Stephens, then a Utah State University meteorology student, hiked into the sinkhole to collect the reading. In an interview with Utah Public Radio decades later , Stephens recalled that those subzero hikes that he took to monitor the station — which he braved in moon boots and snowshoes — occasionally left him with frostbite. It was a much more comfortable — albeit notably bouncy — journey in late July of this year, when scientists with the Utah Climate Center made the voyage in trucks, jostling along the somewhat precarious canyon road as the vehicles occasionally kissed the rocks beneath. With them was András Dobos, a Hungarian scientist who aims to further study the weather phenomenon that often makes the bottoms of sinkholes colder than their rims. Brock Marchant / UPR | The Salt Lake Tribune Hungarian scientist András Dobos, left, and Utah State University graduate research assistant Tim Wright climb the edge of a basin in Logan Canyon to install a temperature sensor on July 29, 2026. It's a concept many Utahns are undoubtedly familiar with: inversions . They happen when a layer of warm air traps cold air below, and in places like the Salt Lake Valley and Cache Valley, they can also trap wintertime pollution. Dobos, whose research spans the globe, wants to know more than the difference between the temperature at the top and bottom of Peter Sinks, as well as other sinks in northern Utah. With the help of the Utah Climate Center, he set up measuring stations at different heights in the limestone bowls. These measurements, he said, will help scientists better understand how the microclimates differ from other geographical basins that host mini inversions. And this, he said, can help Utahns. "In Utah, cold air pools and generally the basin [effect] can impact our daily life," he said in an email. "Understanding these processes can also help with agriculture, forestry, environment protection and adaptation to local climate conditions." Tim Wright — a graduate research assistant at USU's Plants, Soils and Climate Department — said a better understanding of inversions can improve the weather forecasts that predict them. Brock Marchant / UPR | The Salt Lake Tribune Hungarian scientist András Dobos installs temperature sensors at Peter Sinks in Logan Canyon on July 29, 2026. "If the forecasts are improved then more preemptive steps can be made to reduce emissions," he said. "The research can also inform air quality studies in refining how bad air quality can get during inversion episodes." While inversions can't be prevented or mitigated, Wright said, pollution can. And that's something people can act on. Why Peter Sinks' temperature sinks Between navigating difficult patches of the dirt road's grab-handle-testing ruts and rocky ridges, Wright explained the weather anomaly. Here's the simple version: The Earth cools at night. As the air also cools, it flows into sinkholes like water might flow into a depression. Given calm conditions, when there's nothing to clear the sinks out, that dense air can stay at the bottom of the basin and the temperature can vary `significantly from the rim. Dobos, the Hungarian scientist, said his current research isn't about capturing eye-catching (or scientist-frostbiting) temperatures. "It's very important to say that our research is definitely not about the records," he said. Brock Marchant / UPR | The Salt Lake Tribune A temperature sensor installed at Peter Sinks in Logan Canyon. He's more interested in comparing how weather affects sinkholes around the world. His research has also taken him to the Mohos sinkhole in Hungary and sinkholes in the Slovenian Alps. Dobos plans to continue his Peter Sinks research until the middle of next summer. That will be followed by processing, analyzing and publishing the data. What comes then, he said, is still up in the air. Police responded with water ⁠cannon and teargas to disperse protesters who started a fire at the ministry of education building, overturned bins and smashed the fronts of local businesses. A branch of Raiffeisen Bank near the education ministry also caught fire. The protests are the most violent outburst yet against Edi Rama, ⁠the prime minister, who won a fourth term in office in May last year but has since faced ​growing discontent at perceived graft surrounding top ‌officials. Protesters also dismiss opposition figures ‌as unpalatable alternatives. View image in fullscreen Protesters clash with police in central Tirana. Photograph: Adnan Beci/AFP/Getty The unrest caps a summer of peaceful protests against Rama, triggered by the proposed development ‌of a luxury resort along Albania’s pristine southern coast backed by Donald Trump’s son-in-law Jared Kushner, which has been caught up in legal disputes. “This is a revolution. We are tired of peaceful protests. We will not stop until Rama resigns,” said Lora, a student who declined to give her last name as she threw rocks at the police. Others chanted “resignation” and “police of crime”. Student ‌organisers said the protest was over conditions at universities, higher education costs, a lack of financial support and employment prospects after graduation. 1:14 Anti-government student protests in Albania turn violent – video The unrest is part of a ​broader wave of student activism sweeping Europe over education and living conditions. In France, high school students have staged weeks of protests and school blockades demanding more teachers and better facilities, arguing that deteriorating school buildings and overcrowded classrooms are undermining education. Albanian media reported that Wednesday’s protests had spread to universities at Elbasan and Shkodër. Photograph: Florion Goga/Reuters Albana Koçiu, the deputy prime minister of Albania, said on Facebook: “Protesting is a legitimate right, but it cannot be used ​as an excuse for violence, city ​destruction or ugly fighting in the middle ​of the road. I call on ​students and every ‌honest citizen who believes in ​the right to ​protest: distance yourself from violence and vandalism!” The police issued a statement calling for calm. “Any person who uses violence, burns or destroys property, or attacks police officers, bears individual responsibility and will face the law, in accordance with the offences committed,” they said. Meanwhile, the EU, which the Balkan nation aspires to join, voiced concern over what it called the “violent escalation at the protest in Tirana”. A statement by the EU delegation in Tirana said: “We take note of the allegations of excessive violence by the police against protesters and journalists,” Calling for a prompt investigation, the delegation encouraged “all sides to de-escalate the tension”.
